title: Biosecurity in the AI Era
gist: In a RAND podcast, Steph Guerra outlines a nine-mitigation defense-in-depth strategy against AI-enabled bioweapons, stressing monitoring over blocking, digital chokepoints, tiered maturity of safeguards, and US-China cooperation, with urgency despite uncertain measurement of AI bio risk.

insights.claim: RAND frames AI-bio risk in three buckets: bioweapons uplift (lowering technical, operational or motivational barriers), biosecurity circumvention, and bioweapons novelty (designs not found in nature).
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Useful taxonomy for evaluating AI lab safety claims and regulation.
insights.locator: we really think about the risks at the AI-bio intersection in three primary buckets

insights.claim: Scientists showed earlier in 2026 that trained AI models can design entirely new viruses, which infected bacteria rather than humans.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Evidence that generative biology capability is real, raising regulatory pressure on bio-AI tools.
insights.locator: Earlier this year, scientists showed that trained AI models can design entirely new viruses

insights.claim: RAND's worst-case scenarios are events at least 10 times COVID-19, which killed about 7 million confirmed; historical precedents include 1918 influenza (50-100 million), Black Death (50-200 million) and 20th-century smallpox (300-500 million).
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Anchors tail-risk scale used to justify biosecurity spending.
insights.locator: these types of worst case scenarios

insights.claim: Pandemic-scale threats combine moderate pathogenicity, high transmissibility and novelty to the human immune system; AI could add engineered novelty and enable more people to upskill to create such viruses.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: AI lowers the expertise barrier, widening the pool of potential threat actors.
insights.locator: there will be more people that are going to be able to upskill

insights.claim: AI co-scientist agents and bio tools like AlphaFold improve research efficiency but in the wrong hands could lower barriers to dangerous experiments, the core dual-use dilemma.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Same capabilities driving biotech upside create regulatory risk for bio-AI developers.

insights.claim: RAND's strategy layers nine mitigations because no single intervention is bulletproof; together they add friction along the risk pathway to detect, disrupt or deter attackers.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Policy likely to favor layered requirements rather than single-point rules.
insights.quote: no single intervention is going to be bulletproof
insights.locator: In biodefense, we oftentimes are focused

insights.claim: Gene synthesis screening and know-your-customer checks are necessary but insufficient, since state programs have in-house capability and actors can split orders across many providers.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Screening mandates alone will not close the gap; compliance and service demand grows for screening vendors.

insights.claim: Different actors need different defenses: access controls fail against insiders like the Amerithrax perpetrator and state programs, which are better addressed by deterrence through attribution and consequences.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Threat-actor-specific policy mix matters for national security planning.

insights.claim: Misuse monitoring is argued to beat blocking alone because blocked users are alerted and may migrate to open-weight models without safeguards, whereas monitoring preserves visibility and allows more inclusive detection thresholds.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Pushes AI labs toward monitoring and logging, with privacy tradeoffs and open-weight leakage concerns.
insights.locator: the threat actor is not alerted

insights.claim: Misuse monitoring must be privacy-preserving, avoiding human review of individual data unless above a threshold, and can use baselines from trusted-access programs for legitimate virology, immunology and microbiology users.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Privacy design is a prerequisite for adoption and a potential regulatory flashpoint.

insights.claim: The report extends physical chokepoints beyond gene synthesis providers to contract research organizations, automated cloud labs and academic plasmid repositories.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Potential new compliance obligations for cloud labs and CROs.
insights.locator: other emerging suppliers within the biological supply chain

insights.claim: RAND proposes digital chokepoints: protecting sensitive curated biological data (e.g., pandemic influenza) and using managed-access platforms for risky tools and datasets.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Signals a shift of controls upstream to data and tools in bio-AI.

insights.claim: Only a small subset of AI biological tools has the capability to design novel pathogens, per RAND's global risk index, so stringent access controls can be narrowly targeted to preserve open science.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Regulation may be narrow, limiting broad impact on bio-AI startups.
insights.locator: it's a small subset of tools

insights.claim: CEPI launched the Pandemic Preparedness Engine, a managed-access platform for its researchers' tools and data, as an example of frontier AI labs and partners building access control in from the start.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Managed-access is becoming a norm in large AI-bio collaborations.

insights.claim: The nine mitigations span four maturity tiers: nascent (e.g., tamper-resistant safeguards for closed and open-weight models), technically feasible but early, established with implementation gaps (gene synthesis screening), and technically tractable but institutionally complex.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Shows where R&D funding is needed, notably tamper-resistant safeguards.

insights.claim: AI bio risk cannot be tested like cyber risk in a sandbox, so evaluators use proxies and non-hazardous materials and will likely never have full confidence in model capability, yet waiting is argued to be too late.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Policy must act under uncertainty; expect precautionary regulation of frontier models.
insights.quote: if we wait too long until these capabilities are demonstrably effective, it will be too late
insights.locator: The reality is, we likely will never have full confidence

insights.claim: Implementation requires sustained US leadership, industry partnership because labs lead on safeguards and monitoring, and US-China cooperation, since unilateral gene synthesis mandates leave other countries as sources of precursors.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Biosecurity regulation is a US-China geopolitical coordination issue and may trigger standards-setting for AI deployment.
insights.locator: Cooperation between the U.S. and China

insights.claim: Guerra's takeaway is that the time to act is now: mitigations are non-trivial, will take years, and many are longstanding biosecurity asks.
insights.speaker: Steph Guerra
insights.so_what: Expect rising investment and policy attention in AI-bio safeguards.
insights.locator: the time to act is really now
